1:
The rock and the pit are Abraham and Sarah, and nobody disputes it. Clarke says so in a line, having first laid the chapter out as a scheme: Abraham's children exhorted to trust, the Gentiles encouraged to look for a share, the everlasting duration of that salvation described, and Jerusalem at the end in the street under the cup of wrath with none of her own to comfort her. Ellicott states the argument the figure carries: the wonder of Israel's origin is itself the ground for believing in its restoration. Gill reads following after righteousness as the pursuit of a righteousness not one's own, presupposing want, a sense of want, and a sight of the thing wanted lying outside oneself. Henry alone turns the quarry into a doctrine of the first birth, setting beside Ur and the Egyptian slave-gangs the hardness of the rock any man is hewn from, and bidding those now advanced remember how low they began.

Called alone, and blessed, and increased. Ellicott renders it as one, and notes the exiles had learned to invert the argument, boasting that Abraham was one and they were many, so the odds must favour them. Clarke reads it straight as encouragement, that what was made out of one can be restored from a remnant. Wesley makes the loneliness obedience, Abraham following into an unknown land out of all his kindred, his condition desperate to the eye of reason. Henry weighs the two cases: Jacob is very small, but not so small as Abraham was, who nonetheless became father of nations, and the captives in Babylon may take the point. Gill adds that the rock is set there to be imitated as well as remembered.

The comfort is horticultural. Gill lists its channels: the ministry of the word, the ordinances, the promises applied, the presence granted, souls added to the people. Wesley grounds it on the covenant, the wilderness turned garden for Abraham's sake. Ellicott finds the verse interesting differently, as evidence the prophet knew the opening chapters of the first book, paradise having entered by now into the very idea of restoration.

Then a dispute about who is being addressed. Wesley takes my people and my nation for the Jews as a peculiar people. Henry describes them by knowledge and heart, a people who not only have righteousness made known but can judge between good and evil, and have the law written within. Delitzsch keeps Israel as the audience while insisting the work in view runs far past Israel's own restoration. Clarke breaks with them all on manuscript evidence, reading the plurals, ye peoples and ye nations, which makes the address a call of the Gentiles; God nowhere else calls his people my nation, and the corruption follows from a habit of abbreviating the plural ending with a stroke later effaced.

What the righteousness is divides them too. Gill takes it forensically, a righteousness wrought out and revealed and applied. Clarke refuses the narrowing: the word carries justice, truth, faithfulness, goodness, mercy, deliverance and salvation together, and here means the faithful keeping of a promise. Wesley agrees, calling it salvation and the effect of God's justice. Ellicott puts judgment first in the order and conversion after it, the far countries at last trusting the arm that struck them. Then the heavens go: Delitzsch resolves them into atoms like smoke, the inhabitants dying out like a nonentity, and Ellicott adds a rival rendering, dying like gnats, a third comparison beside smoke and garment. Wesley limits the loss to the present state and properties, the substance surviving. Clarke reports Aben Ezra finding the soul's immortality in the verse. Ellicott hears the fear-not spoken to the Israel within Israel; Delitzsch reads the same address as the servant of Jehovah in its middle sense. Gill turns the moth on the revilers themselves, secret and gradual and certain.
9:
Who cries awake, and to whom? Ellicott sets out four candidates, the redeemed and ideal Israel, the Servant, the prophet, and God self-communing after the manner of men, prefers the first, then doubts whether poetry this high admits the distinction. Gill makes it a prayer of the prophet, or rather the church through him, and rejects the versions addressing it to Jerusalem or Zion; the one addressed is the Father, thought asleep when he does not appear, or Christ, who is himself the power of God. Henry allows either, the arm standing for Christ or for God, and explains the figure from the body: a benumbed limb we call asleep, and it wakes when stretched out for use. He grants God needs no reminding, and says the leave to be earnest is given anyway.

The plea is precedent. Henry reads the ancient days as Egypt, plague after plague cutting Rahab to pieces and giving the dragon his death wound, and turns the memory into a rule of prayer: past experience supports faith and may be pleaded. Wesley identifies the pair briskly, Rahab for Egypt from its pride, the dragon for Pharaoh. Ellicott agrees, then reaches outside Scripture entirely, quoting through Cheyne an Egyptian invocation hailing the sun god as one who cut the scorner in pieces and strangled the evil serpent. Gill keeps to the Red Sea and its east wind, adding that the arm which dried that water can dry the Euphrates when the time comes.

Then a promise, and a question where it came from. Ellicott notes the verse repeats an earlier chapter word for word, and puts the choice between the prophet quoting himself and a later writer quoting him; the assumption that a copyist inserted it rests on no adequate ground. Clarke uses the repetition as a tool, collating the passages to recover two verbs the manuscripts and oldest editions support, and concluding a letter here has been misread as the final letter of the word before. Gill offers a third construction, that the sentence continues the prayer rather than answering it; Wesley and Henry take it as the answer, God having done these things and meaning the like again.

The reply comes doubled. Gill hears in the repeated pronoun more than was asked: they prayed for power and are given the Comforter himself, working not through the usual means but immediately. Ellicott makes the doubling a statement of odds: the enemies mortal and weak, the protector eternal and strong. Henry observes God had ordered his ministers to comfort, and takes the work in hand himself because they cannot reach the heart; he notices too that the pronoun in the reproof is feminine, who art thou, O woman, a rebuke to fear unworthy of a man. Wesley hears the oppressor's fury spoken of as gone because it certainly and suddenly will be. Clarke moves a letter from one word to the next on the evidence of the Greek and Latin.

The last verses gather the figures up. Clarke rewrites the hastening captive as a rescuer marching at speed, Cyrus temporally and the Messiah spiritually. Gill keeps the captive but doubles the sense, the time hastening or the prisoner seizing his first opening, and reports the reading that makes him merely impatient. Ellicott takes him for one bowed down in fetters, the pit an underground dungeon where a man was left to starve. Delitzsch marks where the promise leaves history and rises to its full height. On the words put in the mouth, Gill canvasses the church, the prophet and Christ; Wesley says the people, God's word being put in their mouths too; Ellicott refuses both the Servant reading and Cheyne's suspicion of misplacement, holding Israel addressed in its ideal, an ideal filled only by the Servant. Clarke would read stretch out the heavens for plant them, the planting found nowhere else.
17:
The same word occurs twice, meaning two things. Ellicott sets the parallel out: earlier it was spoken to the arm of the Lord and opened a promise, here to Jerusalem as a drunkard, opening a ruin so vivid the call seems prefixed to make it bearable; being called at all shows the ruin is not final. Delitzsch has the second cry grow out of the first, the prophet returning in God's name what the church asked. What sleep is meant divides them. Henry says not so much the sleep of sin as the stupor of despair, the nearest case being disciples sleeping for sorrow. Gill goes further, hearing a summons out of death, the church rising as the witnesses stood on their feet. Wesley keeps it simple: rouse thyself, stand up, thou who wast thrown down.

The cup is the chapter's hardest image. Clarke translates it the cup of mortal poison, thinking of the old practice of despatching criminals by a draught, Socrates sentenced to hemlock. Wesley says the same plainly: a cup that strikes with deadly horror, every drop drunk. Henry works the theology: the cup of fury is a cup of trembling to everyone who takes it, and where the dregs were threatened against the wicked of the earth, Jerusalem has made herself one of them and must wring them out too, a cup of fornication being followed by a cup of fury. Ellicott, soberer, reads the phrase as the goblet drained.

What follows is abandonment. Gill keeps the drunkard staggering in the street with nobody to hold her up, not even her relations. Then the count: two things are named, four words follow, and they divide over the arithmetic. Clarke takes the terms alternately, desolation by famine and destruction by the sword, noting that the Chaldee paraphrast, missing this, said two afflictions had come and four more would. Wesley reaches the same pairing another way, the land wasted and the people destroyed, famine and sword not new evils but the means. Ellicott inverts it, two effects and two causes. Gill alone counts differently, making them the affliction itself and the absence of any friend to bear it.

Then the unanswerable question. Clarke prefers the third person on a manuscript and four versions, who shall comfort thee, and calls it evidently right. Ellicott keeps the first and lets it stand at its worst: even God is shown failing, or seeming to fail, to find her a comforter. Wesley reads a search that comes back empty. The sons are past helping, having drunk the same cup; Ellicott has them lying like corpses in the open places and calls the netted creature an antelope, where Clarke and Lowth make it the oryx in the toils, drenched to the full, and Wesley sees the unkilled still struggling. Drunken but not with wine sends Clarke to Aeschylus on being intoxicated with passion and to Plato's imagined potion that induces fear by the draught; he breaks off to call the passage poetry of the first order.

The reversal is a transfer, not a remission. Gill hears the double title as security, the Lord of all who can do everything and the covenant God who does what he promised, and expects Babylon's fate to fall on the mystical. Ellicott notes the rare plural beside the name, and that God pleads for his people when nobody else will; the cup leaves the castaway's hand for her enemies. Wesley adds that the one who fought against her is reconciled and will maintain her cause. Delitzsch carries the sequence in one breath, from the sons at the street corners to the cup handed on. The last insult is the footstool, and Clarke documents it: feet set on the necks of kings, seventy maimed captives gathering food under a conqueror's table, a Roman emperor stooping so a Persian king could mount from his back.
